newsitem.title: FRANCE: Seguin, Balladur likely favourites to succeed Juppe.
newsitem.headline: Seguin, Balladur likely favourites to succeed Juppe.

text.p: Outgoing National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin or patrician ex-premier Edouard Balladur are likely favourites to succeed Prime Minister Alain Juppe if the centre-right keeps power in France's snap election.

Stunned by Sunday's first round of a parliamentary election in which the left won more votes than the ruling centre-right, Juppe said on Monday he would step down irrespective of the outcome of the June 1 runoff.
An opinion poll this month showed that 26 percent of voters favoured the gruff Seguin as next prime minister if the centre-right wins, 21 percent Balladur and just eight percent Juppe.
The following are portraits of leading candidates:
PHILIPPE SEGUIN, 54
A bearlike figure with a strong temper, Seguin led the "no" campaign against the Maastricht treaty on European Union before French voters narrowly approved the treaty in a 1992 referendum.
The former social affairs minister has since cautiously endorsed plans for the single European currency, all the while pushing for more efforts to create jobs and help the poor.
"We must certainly launch the single European currency; the French people have so decided," he said during the campaign. A year ago, he wrote that the euro was "the false prophets' new Holy Grail".
A former law lecturer and an outstanding orator, he advocates a more expansionary economic policy and criticised Juppe for putting the fight for jobs second to budget austerity.
EDOUARD BALLADUR, 68
Appointing Balladur would be a bitter pill for Chirac, who beat Balladur for the presidency in 1995 after a fratricidal battle between the two former conservative friends.

Aristocratic, soft-spoken but sharp-minded, Balladur has been propelled back into the limelight after a reconciliation handshake with Chirac last month. Unlike Seguin, the silver-haired Balladur advocates more free-market policies.

"France must make a clearer shift in a liberal direction in its economic and social policies," he said. "This means less spending, smaller deficits, lower taxes, more contracts, more dialogue, more freedom, more flexibility."

Balladur worked his way up the hierarchy almost unnoticed to emerge in 1993 as prime minister in a centre-right government "cohabiting" with Socialist president Francois Mitterrand. Chirac, who won the presidency in 1995,named Juppe as his replacement.
FRANCOIS LEOTARD, 55
Leader of France's second largest political force, the Union for French Democracy (UDF), Leotard has set his sights on the French presidency but time and again has seen his hopes dashed.

Leotard is an economic liberal and a strong supporter of closer European Union integration. His chequered career has included stints as defence minister under Balladur and as culture minister when Chirac was prime minister from 1986-88.
FRANCOIS BAYROU, 46

A high-flying academic turned education minister, centrist Bayrou is a smooth negotiator and persuasive television performer. The daily Le Monde once described him as "skilled at reconciling the unreconcilable and at avoiding controversy".

Bayrou entered politics at 21 and climbed rapidly to become one of the youngest faces in Balladur's coalition cabinet in 1993. He stayed on as education minister under Juppe. A former schoolteacher, Bayrou is a devout Catholic and pro-European.
RAYMOND BARRE, 73
Prime minister from 1976 to 1981, Barre built his career on remaining an outsider and prides himself on speaking blunt truths.

Strongly pro-European, the rotund ex-economics professor's textbooks trained generations of students. He has retained high popularity, helped by jibes at the political establishment. He once called French politicians "clowns" out of touch with the country.
